answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1867–1934 · Physicist and chemist; two-time Nobel laureate
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Marie Curie and consistent with a view she is documented to have expressed — “In science, we should be interested in things, not persons” (1923) — but no primary source pins this exact wording, which reads as a modern paraphrase. Wikiquote lists it with no citation ↗.

source.excerpt: Be less curious about people and more curious about ideas.
trail: The sourced Curie sentiment first appears in 1923, in Marie Mattingly Meloney’s introduction to Curie’s Pierre Curie (Macmillan): “In science, we should be interested in things, not persons,” as traced by Quote Investigator ↗.
The popular reworded aphorism is carried by Wikiquote ↗ with no source, book, or date attached.
It has spread widely as a verbatim quote — over a thousand Goodreads likes ↗ — on a page the site marks as community-added and unverified.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular wording is a paraphrase, not a documented quote
source.excerptNote: No book, letter, or speech has been found containing this sentence. The nearest documented statement is one journalist Marie Mattingly Meloney recorded in 1923: Curie, correcting a reporter’s interest in her private life, said “In science, we should be interested in things, not persons.” Curie herself credited that principle to her husband, Pierre. The familiar “curious about people / curious about ideas” phrasing appears to be a much later aphoristic reworking of that idea.

source.rightsNote: The documented 1923 cognate (“In science, we should be interested in things, not persons”) is public domain. The exact reworded aphorism has no identifiable author or date, so its provenance — not its copyright — is the open question.

author.name: Marie Curie
author.heading: Who was Marie Curie?
author.metaLine: 1867–1934 · Physicist and chemist; two-time Nobel laureate
author.bio: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867, Marie Curie was a pioneer of research on radioactivity — a term she coined. She won the Nobel Prize in Physics (1903), shared with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry (1911), becoming the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two sciences. Famously indifferent to fame and money, she repeatedly steered public attention away from her person and toward her work — the very attitude this quote tries to capture.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is less a wrong-person mix-up than a wording problem: a genuine Curie idea has been polished into a snappy quote she is not documented to have said in these words.

items.scope: Origin of the underlying idea sometimes traced to
items.why: In her 1923 biography Pierre Curie, Marie attributed the principle — “in science we should be interested in things and not in persons” — to her husband, per Quote Investigator ↗, which concludes the saying is best ascribed to both Curies.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: a real Curie sentiment, first documented in 1923, later reworded into a quote she is not on record as saying — see the full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line endures because it distils a real trait of Curie’s: an almost total impatience with celebrity and gossip, and a conviction that science should be about phenomena rather than personalities. She lived it — declining to patent radium, shrinking from the press, and, when a reporter pressed her about herself, redirecting the conversation to the work.
That the exact aphorism is a later paraphrase rather than her documented words doesn’t make it dishonest — but on a provenance site it earns amber, not green.
context.pull: A genuine Curie idea, polished into words she is not on record as saying.
